title: Paying $120 to cover a $100 risk
hook: Insurance costs more than the average loss. So why does anyone buy it?

doesNotKnow: how to find the average payout (chance × loss)
why paying more than the average loss can still be sensible

misconception: If insurance costs more than the average loss, it is a rip-off.
objective: The learner can compute an expected loss as chance times size, explain that a premium above it covers the insurer's costs, and explain that insurance swaps a small certain cost for protection from a rare large loss that a pool of many customers can absorb.

claims.text: A 1-in-100 chance a year of a $10,000 loss means an average payout of $100 per customer a year.
A $120 premium is $20 above the average loss; in this model that $20 covers the insurer's costs.
claims.source: 120 − 100 = 20. 'Covers the insurer's costs' is the model's assumption (brief), not a claim about real insurers' margins.

claims.text: With 100 independent houses, single years are lumpy: a year has no loss about 37% of the time and two or more about 26% of the time.
On the stage, one seeded run: the first year has exactly one loss, and over the first 101 years the average payout is $99 per customer a year (36 years with no loss, 28 with two or more).
claims.source: Demo.tsx HISTORY with mulberry32(seed 1), one draw per house per year, loss if < 0.01. Seed 1 was CHOSEN because its first year has exactly one loss, as in the brief. Across 2,000 seeds the 101-year average is $100 on average, 95% between $80 and $120; for seed 1, every average from 50 to 1,001 years lies between $88 and $107.

claims.text: Insurance swaps a small certain cost for protection from a rare large loss, and an insurer can carry the risk because it pools many customers.
claims.source: Risk pooling and risk aversion as the basis of insurance markets (N. G. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, ch. 27, 'The Market for Insurance'). Law of large numbers: the per-customer average over many independent risks approaches the expected loss.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: independent risks, no fraud, one premium; it gives no advice about buying cover.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own simulation, shown on the stage chip and in the reveal.

recall.question: A phone has a 1-in-20 chance a year of a $400 repair. A plan costs $30 a year. What is the average repair cost per phone a year?
recall.why: Average loss = chance × size = 1/20 × $400 = $20. The $30 plan is $10 above it: you pay that for not facing the $400 surprise.
